title: Mountie kills knife-wielding mom
article: A 40-year-old woman was shot and killed by an RCMP officer responding to a domestic disturbance call in the remote community of Alert Bay Friday night.
Around 8 p.m., a Mountie fired a single shot when the woman confronted him with a butcher knife, said Sgt. Lee Omilusik.

The woman was identified by locals as Lorraine Moon, who also went by the name Lorraine Jacobson. She was pronounced dead at Alert Bay Hospital after community members said she was shot in front of her nine-year-old daughter Summer. But police couldn't confirm whether the girl or a son Lance, 11, were in the home at the time.

"She started coming toward the member who feared for his safety," Omilusik said. "He attempted to disarm her, give her some verbal commands to put the knife down and when attempts failed ... he was left with no other option but to fire a single shot, which hit her."

Omilusik said the constable was alone when he went into the home. Another officer was heading to the scene for backup when the shooting happened. The officers called for an ambulance but instead decided to take her to hospital in a patrol car to save time, he said.
Omilusik wouldn't say where the woman was shot. Community members said she was shot in the chest.
"They tried to get her over there as quickly as they could for treatment," Omilusik said.
The incident occurred in a home on the Whe la la U First Nations community on Cormorant Island, off the coast of Vancouver Island near Port MacNeill.
The constable was identified by community members as Russ Chanin. Police haven't officially released the name of the officer, who was said to have a year's experience.

Police aren't sure what the reason was for the initial domestic disturbance call, or who had called for help. At the time of the shooting there was a man in the house, described by Omilusik as a friend.
Police said the woman had recently moved to the area after living in the Comox Valley.
Alert Bay Mayor Gilbert Popovich said the shooting was the talk of the close-knit town. "It's a hell of a shock," he said. "It's one of those things that leave you stunned."
William Cranmer, chief of the Namgis First Nation near Whe la la U, said the community has been left to question their relationship with police officers.

"Members are quite angry that something like this would have happened," he said. "I guess that (police) have to review their policy because there's a person that's dead and we wonder if it was necessary."
Cranmer said the relations between the citizens and the small four-member Alert Bay RCMP detachment have been smooth in the past, though he said the shooting tells them there's need for change.
"We're going to have to figure out some better working relationship with the police," he said.
Meanwhile, both the constable who fired the Smith and Wesson nine- millimetre weapon and the traumatized community are working with counsellors to cope with the aftermath.

"We have a force psychologist who will be speaking to him, because it's a pretty traumatic situation," said Omilusik about the officer. "They sit down and go over the situation and make sure that things are as normal as they can be under the circumstances."
The Namgis health centre has made all its staff available to anyone in the community who needs to talk about the shooting, Cranmer said.
Courtenay RCMP's major crime unit is heading up the investigation, along with the provincial coroner's office.
"We'll be taking witness statements and interviewing all the neighbours and interviewing anyone that had anything to do with this unfortunate incident," Omilusik said.
In a police shooting, he said, it is standard practice for a coroner's inquest to be performed after the police investigation is finished.
Cranmer said they plan to hold an open meeting in the recreation centre on Whe la la U on Tuesday for community members to talk about the shooting.
